To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Bouguer anomalies of complex craters in lunar highlands are negative, though positive Bouguer anomaly values are observed, especially in the case of smaller craters, and that the crater Bouguer anomaly is inversely correlated with crater diameter.

(1) impact cratering produces a negative gravity anomaly that scales inversely with crater size, and that (2) impact cratering is the dominant mechanism of lunar crustal porosity production and is in a state of saturation for craters larger than ~93km in diameter.
the lunar highlands have a ~8km thick megaregolith with a porosity of ~10%, and that the megaregolith is saturated with impact porosity for craters larger than ~30km diameter.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the origin of the lunar highlands and the role of impact cratering on their structure and composition.
the production and saturation of porosities in lunar highlands from complex cratering.
the production of porosity in impact craters.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
impact cratering has created a highly porous, fractured, and heterogeneous lunar crust, with a maximum porosity of ~10%.
the lunar highlands are highly porous, and that this porosity was created by impact cratering.

the Bouguer gravity of the complex craters on the Moon is a function of the size of the impactor, and the depth of the megaregolith is about 8km, and it has not changed much since the formation of the Moon, and the Moon is still in a state of impact equilibrium.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lunar highlands are in a state of porosity saturation, with the largest impact basins being the only features that can produce significant additional porosity.
the Moon is a fractured body.

the Bouguer gravity signature of the Moon is the result of the combined effect of the crustal thickness, the density contrast between the crust and mantle, the impact history, and the depth to which the lunar megaregoloth is fractured.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Moon is not a homogeneous body.
the BA of complex craters is a sensitive indicator of the depth of impact-generated porosity and can be used to infer the porosity of the lunar crust.

the lunar highlands are a complex, fractured system with a porosity that has evolved over time, and that the cratering history of the lunar surface can be quantitatively reconstructed from its gravity field.
